Education is not preparation for life but a continuing part of it. The young are not empty vessels awaiting fill; they are already living beings with impulses, interests, and habits, and the task of schooling is to give those capacities worthy direction. A school that treats children as passive recipients will produce docile adults, whereas a school that invites them to inquire and test ideas will produce citizens capable of self-government. This does not mean the abandonment of discipline or subject matter; it means that discipline must grow out of purposeful activity and that knowledge must be connected to experience. Growth, in this sense, is both the means and the end of education — there is no goal beyond it to which it is subordinate.
